prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. The case for it is not nostalgia, and it does not rest on the idea that neat writing is a mark of character. It rests on a few plain facts about what children have to do in school, how long they will be expected to do it with a pen, and what is lost when a skill is dropped because it looks old. A child who can write quickly and legibly by hand has one less thing to think about when the real work begins, which is deciding what to say. Joined writing is the usual route to that speed, and it takes a few years of steady teaching to arrive there.

It helps to start with what is actually asked of children. The national curriculum for England, introduced in 2014, expects pupils in Year 2, aged six and seven, to begin using the diagonal and horizontal strokes that join letters. In Years 3 and 4 they are meant to use those joins with confidence and to understand which adjacent letters are better left unjoined. By the end of Year 6 the writing assessment expects pupils to maintain legibility in joined handwriting when writing at speed. That is a modest standard. Nobody is asking ten-year-olds for copperplate. The requirement is that a child can fill a page in reasonable time and that another person can read it afterwards.

The argument against has real force, and it should be stated fairly. Finland removed compulsory cursive from its national curriculum in 2016 and asked schools to teach typing instead. In the United States the Common Core standards of 2010 left cursive out, and many states followed that lead for a time. Typing is also a skill every child will need, and a child of seven today will spend far more of adult life at a keyboard than holding a pen. Teaching time in primary school is finite, and an hour spent on joins is an hour not spent on reading, number or science. If joined writing were only a matter of appearance, those arguments would be enough to settle the question.

It is not only a matter of appearance. Handwriting is a motor skill that has to become automatic before it stops competing with other demands. A child who must stop to think about how to form each letter has less attention left for spelling, sentence structure and the content of the sentence. Researchers such as Steve Graham in the United States have found over many studies that handwriting fluency in the primary years predicts the length and quality of children's later written compositions. This is the central point. Fluency does not make a child a better thinker, but slow and laboured letter formation limits how much of that thinking reaches the page. Children who struggle to write tend to write less, and teachers then have less to work with.

Joining letters is the natural way to build that fluency. When a word is written as one continuous movement, the pen leaves the paper less often, and the hand learns the shape of the whole word rather than a string of separate marks. Print is easier to start with, and nobody disputes that children should learn it first. But print asks for a lift and a restart at every letter, and that sets a ceiling on speed. Some children find their own mixture of joined and unjoined forms by the age of eleven or twelve, and the curriculum's wording about leaving some letters unjoined allows for this. The view taken here is that it is easier to arrive at a personal, partly joined hand having been taught the joins than to arrive there with no guidance at all.

There is also evidence about what handwriting does for learning beyond speed. Virginia Berninger and colleagues compared children in Years 2, 4 and 6 writing by pen and by keyboard, and found that the children wrote more words and expressed more ideas when they used a pen. A 2005 study by Marieke Longcamp and colleagues found that young children who practised letters by hand recognised them better afterwards than children who practised on a keyboard. These findings are not conclusive. The much-quoted 2014 study by Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer, which found that students taking notes by hand did better on conceptual questions than those typing, has had mixed results on replication. It would be wrong to claim that the science proves handwriting makes children cleverer. What it supports is a smaller claim, that writing by hand is not a poorer tool than typing in the early years and may be a better one while the child is still learning the letters.

The strongest practical argument is the simplest. Pupils in England still sit their GCSE and A-level examinations on paper, in handwriting, with only a small number given permission to use a laptop. Those who cannot write fast enough in an exam hall lose marks for answers they never finished or that the examiner could not read. A student who has spent three hours writing by hand for a paper needs a hand that will last three hours. Whatever one thinks of exams as a way of testing, they are the system children will meet, and a school that stopped teaching a skill the system demands would be doing those children no favour. It is possible that exams will move to screens in the next decade or two. They have not yet, and children now in Year 1 will reach their GCSEs in the early 2030s.

Handwriting matters outside school too, though less than it once did. Adults still fill in forms, sign documents, write cards, leave notes and take down messages. They write shopping lists and phone numbers on whatever is at hand. A person who cannot produce legible joined writing at a reasonable speed is not shut out of modern life, but will find some ordinary tasks slower and more awkward than they need to be. This is a minor argument next to the others, and it should be kept in proportion, but it is not nothing.

The place where I think the case is most often misjudged is in the treatment of children who find writing hard. It is sometimes said that joined writing is an extra burden for children with dyslexia or poor fine motor control, and that print or typing would serve them better. Some teachers and specialists hold this view and it should not be dismissed. Others argue the opposite. The British Dyslexia Association has said that joined writing can help some dyslexic children because the continuous movement reduces reversals and gives each word a single outline. Where specialists disagree, the sensible policy is to teach joining as the default and make adjustments for the individual child, including keyboards where a child's difficulty is severe. A default that fits most children, with room for exceptions, is better than abolishing the skill for everyone because it is hard for a few.

That leaves the question of how much time to spend. The answer is not a great deal. Ten or fifteen minutes of short, frequent practice a day in the early years does more than a long weekly lesson, because the aim is to build a habit in the hand. It also does not need to come at the expense of keyboard skills. Finland's decision was framed as a choice between the two, but nothing about the timetable requires that. Children can learn to touch type in Years 5 and 6 and still have learnt to join their letters in Years 2 to 4. A school that taught both would give its pupils two working tools in place of one.

It is worth being clear about the limits of this position. Joined handwriting is not a moral good, and a child whose writing is untidy is not careless or unintelligent. Schools that spend lessons on perfecting slant and spacing, or that mark children down for style, are missing the point. The goal is a hand that is legible, comfortable and fast enough not to get in the way. A modest, regular programme of teaching, with attention paid to pencil grip and posture, is enough to reach it for most children.

The reasons for continuing are, in the end, quite ordinary. Joined writing builds the fluency that lets children put their ideas down without effort. It is the skill that exams and much everyday paperwork still call for, and the research that exists points to handwriting as a useful tool and not a hindrance. The cost in lesson time is small and the loss, if the skill is dropped, would fall hardest on the children who have the least chance of learning it at home. Until the exam hall and the world outside it change, primary schools should keep teaching children to join their letters.
